questions.q: What is the execArgv option in Node.js child_process.fork()?
o: The working directory for the child process
An array of Node.js CLI flags passed to the child process at startup, such as --inspect or --eval
The environment variables inherited by the child
The maximum memory limit for the child process
questions.x: execArgv lets fork() pass the same kind of CLI flags you would type before a script name, like node --eval 'code' app.js. The child Node process receives and applies those flags during its boot sequence.
questions.h: Think about flags you pass directly to the node command. fork() can pass the same kind of flags to a child through this options field.

questions.q: Why can a polluted Object.prototype.execArgv become an RCE gadget?
o: fork() always runs execArgv values as shell commands directly
If the options object passed to fork() has no own execArgv property, a property lookup can inherit the polluted value from Object.prototype and pass attacker-controlled CLI flags to the child
execArgv overrides the Node.js version at runtime
Object.prototype is writable by default in all Node.js applications
questions.x: When application code calls fork(script, args, options) without setting options.execArgv, the lookup walks the prototype chain. A polluted Object.prototype.execArgv becomes the child's Node CLI flags on older Node.js versions that read options via prototype chain lookup.
questions.h: The options object has no own execArgv. Where else might JavaScript look for that property?

questions.q: Which Node.js CLI flag is most useful for turning execArgv pollution into code execution?
o: --version
--eval or -e, which runs arbitrary JavaScript during child process startup
--help
--max-old-space-size
questions.x: The --eval flag makes the child Node process execute JavaScript code immediately on startup. From that code, require('child_process').execSync() can run OS commands, turning prototype pollution into remote code execution.
questions.h: You need a flag that runs JavaScript before the worker script loads. Which node flag is used for one-liner code execution?

questions.q: On which Node.js versions did the execArgv prototype pollution gadget work without application code copying the value?
o: All Node.js versions including the latest LTS
Versions before 18.18.0 and 20.6.0, where child_process read options properties including those on the prototype chain
Only Node.js 4.x and earlier
Only when running on Windows
questions.x: Starting in Node.js 18.18.0 and 20.6.0, child_process only honors own properties on the options object. Before that, inherited Object.prototype.execArgv was treated as a real option and passed to the child as CLI flags.
questions.h: A Node.js security fix changed how fork() reads options properties. The gadget worked when lookups followed the prototype chain.

questions.q: What is the correct mitigation when calling fork() or spawn() in code that might run alongside polluted Object.prototype?
o: Disable all child_process functions
Set execArgv explicitly to process.execArgv or an empty array on the options object so lookups do not fall through to Object.prototype
Run Node.js with the --no-prototype flag
Only use spawn() with shell: true instead of fork()
questions.x: Assigning execArgv as an own property on the options object prevents prototype chain lookup from reaching a polluted Object.prototype.execArgv. Using process.execArgv or [] ensures predictable, safe CLI flags for the child.
questions.h: The attack works because execArgv is missing as an own property. What is the simplest way to stop the lookup from reaching Object.prototype?
